Hashing and Verifying with bcrypt →

Why Plaintext Passwords Are a Liability

Laravel's Hash facade did this for you automatically. Node doesn't — so it's finally worth seeing done by hand.

User.password has held a literal string — 'placeholder-not-hashed' — for every seeded user since Lesson 2, with a comment on the schema column promising real hashing "arrives in Week 4." That's now. The reasoning itself isn't new: you already know from Laravel why a password column should never hold what a user actually typed — if the database were ever read by someone who shouldn't (a leaked backup, a compromised query, a careless log line), a plaintext password column hands every single user's real password straight to them, and most people reuse passwords across sites, so the damage doesn't even stay contained to this one API.

What's different here is that Laravel's Hash::make()/Hash::check() quietly handled hashing for you, behind Auth::attempt() and friends. Node and Express have no equivalent baked in — there's no framework-provided "user" concept at all, so hashing is something this project's own code has to do explicitly, the same way services, validation, and error handling all turned out to be by-hand infrastructure this project builds rather than inherits. bcrypt (the library, not a hand-rolled hash function) is what this project reaches for — the next slide is what actually calling it looks like.
